Appendix A: Literature review

This appendix adds detail to Section 4 by theme. Each entry in the bibliography records what was read: full text, abstract only, or the bibliographic record.

A.1 Border carbon adjustment design and recognition of foreign effort

The design literature treats recognition of foreign policy as one of a handful of core choices. Ismer and Neuhoff (2007) set out the early case that border adjustment for an emissions trading system can be made consistent with trade law if it is based on best available technology rather than actual foreign emissions. Cosbey et al. (2019), reviewing the literature for practitioners, list the regulatory choices: scope, the method for carbon content, the type and price of the adjustment, scenarios requiring modification, use of revenue, and compliance with trade and climate agreements. Mehling et al. (2019) give the most complete legal-economic analysis, tracing the Commission’s 2008 proposal that would have exempted partners taking “comparable action”; their analysis of the trade-law exceptions is the basis of Section 9. Kortum and Weisbach (2017) ask which goods, emissions and countries a border adjustment should cover, and conclude that adjustments impose high administrative costs and need stronger welfare justifications.

The two closest designs bracket this paper’s proposal. Mehling and Ritz (2023) propose a voluntary individual adjustment: a default intensity that a firm may rebut with its actual intensity, and a top-up charge on the shortfall of the foreign explicit carbon price, \(\max\{t - t_k, 0\} \times \min\{z, Z\}\). They do not include “effective” prices from non-price policies. Equation equation 2 with \(\rho = 0\) and plant-level \(\hat e\) is their rule; the paper’s generalization is to credit the signal and measure by country and sector. Neuhoff et al. (2026) go the other way: standardized values independent of process or location, free allocation at benchmark for EU producers, and a standardized liability per tonne of material, with export relief. That removes shuffling and keeps carbon-pricing incentives along the EU value chain, but by their own account creates no direct incentive for cleaner production or carbon pricing abroad. The country-sector route of Section 7 sits between the two: no plant can shuffle, and the exporting country is rewarded for its own instrument.

Recent work recommends starting simple and moving to finer measurement. Keen et al. (2022) judge border adjustments the most effective unilateral instrument against competitiveness loss and leakage, but stress that design is decisive. They recommend limiting coverage to energy-intensive, trade-exposed sectors, benchmarking initially on domestic emission intensities, and deciding explicitly how to treat partners that mitigate by other means. They show that output-based rebating of a carbon tax is a feebate, the equivalence this paper uses. Clausing and Wolfram (2023) separate free-riding by low-ambition countries from the competitive disadvantage of jurisdictions that price carbon against those that subsidize clean production, and show that one border instrument cannot address both. A feebate, which prices at the margin and subsidizes on average, sits between their two cases, which is why price-paid recognition misjudges it.

Leakage estimates bound what is at stake. Branger and Quirion (2014)’s meta-analysis of 25 studies and 310 estimates finds leakage rates of 5–25 percent without border adjustment (mean 14 percent) and 5–15 percent with it (mean 6 percent); extending the adjustment to all sectors is the most effective feature. Fischer and Fox (2012) compare border adjustment with output-based rebating as anti-leakage tools.

A.2 Who bears CBAM

Exposure falls disproportionately on middle- and low-income exporters with weak verification capacity. Beaufils et al. (2023) find that middle- and low-income countries for which the EU is an important market are hit hardest relative to their economies, even under conservative designs, and explore international schemes for recycling the revenue. Magacho et al. (2024) find Russia, China, Türkiye and Ukraine most exposed in absolute terms, many developing economies with more than 2 percent of exports and 1 percent of production affected, and the Western Balkans, Mozambique, Zimbabwe and Cameroon most exposed relative to their economies. Eicke et al. (2021) build a risk index that includes capacity for monitoring, reporting and verification, and find most high-risk countries in Africa. Perdana and Vielle (2022) find in a general equilibrium model that CBAM cuts leakage by about a third by 2040 but reduces welfare in the least developed countries through lower exports; exempting them raises leakage more than alternatives, while returning revenue for clean energy improves their welfare at low cost to the EU. Mattoo et al. (2009) show, for border taxes set on each exporter’s carbon content, that the burden falls heavily on poorer exporters: China’s manufacturing exports fall by about a fifth, and those of low- and middle-income countries by about 8 percent. These findings matter for recognition because the countries most exposed are those least able to file verified plant data, for which the default values and default carbon prices are the only routes.

A.3 Resource shuffling and leakage under incomplete regulation

The quantitative evidence on shuffling comes from electricity. Fowlie (2009) simulates California’s electricity market under source-based cap-and-trade and finds that exempting out-of-state producers achieves about a third of the reductions of complete regulation at more than twice the cost per tonne. Caron et al. (2015) find that California’s program without restrictions on imported electricity would raise emissions elsewhere by 45 percent of its domestic reduction; with imports in the cap and resource shuffling banned as legislated, leakage falls to 9 percent. The 9 percent assumes the ban works, and Mehling and Ritz (2023) report that it has been difficult to enforce. Fowlie and Reguant (2022) show how to calibrate output subsidies to leakage risk in incomplete carbon markets, which bears on how free-allocation benchmarks should be set. Apaydın (2026) shows the same gap between reported and real cuts in a new place: under CBAM’s electricity-accounting rules, Chinese industrial parks can report reductions of which only about a fifth to a quarter are real in some provinces.

The leading analysis of industrial goods expects less shuffling than in electricity, but offers no measurement. Mehling and Ritz (2023) judge reshuffling “perhaps most acute for electricity markets” and likely less pronounced for industrial goods, whose flows are easier to trace, and suggest a company-level point of regulation. This paper’s Proposition 6 formalizes their trade-off, and the firm-level verification route in Section 7 is their remedy. Their expectation of smaller industrial shuffling is plausible for routing that requires changing physical flows. It is weaker for routing between installations owned by one firm, which requires only that the firm choose which plant fills which order, and for selection into country-average default values, which requires nothing at all.

For steel there are scenario estimates and no measurement of routing. Assous et al. (2024) estimate CBAM fees on imports from China at 2021 trade volumes and full phase-in: €590 million with unchanged flows, €313 million if exporters supply the EU only with electric-furnace steel (half scrap and half direct-reduced or pig iron for flat products), aluminum made with 80 percent scrap and cement with 20 percent clinker, and €695 million with no reporting. They note that the Commission must monitor resource shuffling under Article 30 but has no enforcement mechanism. Hamidani (2026) tests, with monthly customs data for 52 flat-steel products in January–June 2026, whether origins with higher default-based exposure lost EU business, and finds no stable effect yet. A Crossref search on 31 October 2026 found no empirical paper on routing between scrap-EAF and BF-BOF output to the EU.

A.4 Measuring carbon prices beyond explicit ones

Implicit carbon pricing through fuel taxes and subsidies is most of the world’s carbon price, and measures of it exist. Agnolucci et al. (2024) develop a total carbon price that adds indirect pricing, fuel excise taxes net of subsidies, to explicit carbon taxes and emissions trading, for 142 countries from 1991 to 2021. Direct pricing covers roughly a quarter of global emissions, but the global total carbon price is not much higher than in 1994, and indirect pricing still makes up “the lion’s share”. Many developing countries, especially net fuel importers, contribute substantially once indirect pricing counts. Black et al. (2023) estimate efficient fuel prices that reflect supply and environmental costs, and the subsidies implied by charging less. The OECD’s effective carbon rates add carbon taxes, fuel excise taxes and permit prices by country and sector (OECD 2023). All three measure the average price per tonne. Paper 6.1 converts any instrument, including feebates and standards, into the uniform tax that would cut emissions as much, and separates the fuel-switching margin from the demand margin (Stretton 2026d); its switching-margin price is the price signal in equation 2.

A.5 Intensity-based pricing and refunding

Instruments that price intensity and return revenue by output are well understood, and are exactly what price-paid recognition misses. Output-based allocation, tradable performance standards and feebates charge the full rate on emissions at the margin while returning revenue in proportion to output, so they subsidize output relative to a tax (Fischer 2001; Fischer and Fox 2012). Holland et al. (2009) show that an intensity standard can even raise emissions when its implicit output subsidy is large. Paper 1.2 of this series designs feebates for power and industry (Stretton 2026c). Hagem et al. (2020) compare refunding emission payments by output with refunding in proportion to abatement spending: expenditure-based refunding needs a lower fee than a tax for the same abatement, output-based refunding a higher one, and both tilt effort toward abatement technology rather than output. This is the economic content of the draft implementing regulation’s Article 8(2) exemption for revenue-financed decarbonization support, and the basis of the support test in Section 6.2.

A.6 Trade law and comparable effort

The trade-law literature favors recognizing foreign effort and warns against treating like products differently by origin. Ismer and Neuhoff (2007) argue that a border adjustment levied as an internal charge can be defended under the GATT if it charges imports no more than domestic producers would pay with the best available technology. Mehling et al. (2019) analyze the full chain: whether a carbon border charge is an internal tax adjustable at the border, whether products differing only in how they were made are “like”, and the general exceptions of Article XX, whose chapeau forbids “arbitrary or unjustifiable discrimination between countries where the same conditions prevail”. The US–Shrimp disputes are the main precedent: the Appellate Body faulted an import ban that in effect required exporting countries to adopt the same program as the United States, and later accepted a revised measure that required a program comparable in effectiveness (WTO Appellate Body 1998, 2001). For recognition, a test of comparable effect, applied by criteria any country can meet, is safer than one that credits only instruments resembling the importer’s own.

Country-level measures raise their own trade-law questions. Country-specific default values and default carbon prices treat like products differently by origin, which engages most-favored-nation treatment under Article I. Cosbey et al. (2019) and Keen et al. (2022) recommend generous defaults that individual producers can rebut with their own data. The country-sector route of Section 7 departs from this by removing the individual rebuttal for countries that opt in; its defense is that the exporting government chooses it, that the criteria are origin-neutral, and that the verification route stays open to every other exporter. Whether that defense would hold has not been tested.

A.7 What this paper adds

Four points stand against the literature and the legal texts. First, the default carbon price is the operative recognition route for most exporters, and the law makes it discretionary, from 2027, and confines it to countries with carbon pricing rules; for countries with only implicit pricing it is zero by construction. Second, the draft implementing regulation’s Article 8(1)(b)(ii) nets below-baseline emissions, so a feebate or output-based pricing system is recognized only on emissions above its benchmark, although its marginal signal is the full rate; Proposition 4 formalizes this. Third, plant-level measurement creates two routes to shuffling, routing under actual values and selection into country-average default values, neither of which the Commission’s anti-circumvention proposal addresses, while country-sector measurement removes both but leaves plants almost no incentive (Propositions 1–3 and 6). Fourth, a liability formula that credits the country-sector price signal is invariant to shuffling, restores the plant incentive through the exporter’s own instrument and preserves the best-response property of paper 1.1, at a cost to the level playing field that Section 6.1 makes explicit.

Appendix B: Proofs

Proposition 1. The plant-level bill \(B(x) = \tau[e_S x + e_B(Q_{EU} - x)]\) has \(B'(x) = -\tau(e_B - e_S) < 0\). With routing cost \(c\) per tonne moved, the net gain from moving a tonne is \(\tau(e_B - e_S) - c > 0\), so the exporter sets \(x\) at its upper bound \(\min(q_S, Q_{EU})\). The saving relative to \(x_0 = sQ_{EU}\) is \(B(x_0) - B(x^*) = \tau(e_B - e_S)[\min(q_S, Q_{EU}) - sQ_{EU}]\), gross of routing costs. If \(q_S \ge Q_{EU}\) this is \(\tau(e_B - e_S)(1-s)Q_{EU}\); substituting \(e_B = (\bar e - s e_S)/(1-s)\) gives \(\tau(\bar e - e_S)Q_{EU}\). If \(q_S < Q_{EU}\) it is \(\tau(e_B - e_S)\,s\,(Q - Q_{EU})\). Total emissions \(e_B q_B + e_S q_S\) do not depend on \(x\). When \(q_S \ge Q_{EU}\), \(x^* = Q_{EU}\) and \(B = \tau e_S Q_{EU}\), so \(\partial B/\partial e_B = 0\). In the stylized example, \(\tau(e_B - e_S)(1-s)Q_{EU} = 80 \times 1.6 \times 0.8 \times 1 = 102.4\) (€ million).

Proposition 2. Reported embodied carbon in EU imports falls by \((e_B - e_S)\Delta\) because \(\Delta\) tonnes previously supplied at \(e_B\) are now supplied at \(e_S\). Globally, the exporter’s emissions fall by \((e_B - e_S)\Delta\) if the new scrap-EAF output replaces its own BF-BOF output. Of the \(\Delta\) tonnes of scrap used, \(\theta\Delta\) are newly collected and \((1-\theta)\Delta\) are diverted from other users, who replace their scrap-based output at intensity \(e_R\), raising their emissions by \((e_R - e_S)(1-\theta)\Delta\). The net change is \(-(e_B - e_S)\Delta + (1-\theta)(e_R - e_S)\Delta\), equal to \(-\theta(e_B - e_S)\Delta\) when \(e_R = e_B\) and zero when also \(\theta = 0\). Pure rerouting leaves every plant’s output unchanged, so world emissions are unchanged for any \(\theta\).

Proposition 3. (i) \(B_C = \tau\bar e Q_{EU}\) with \(\bar e = \sum_i q_i e_i / Q\) contains no routing variable; every plant is charged at \(\bar e\), so the choice between actual and default values does not arise. (ii) \(\partial B_C/\partial e_i = \tau Q_{EU} q_i/Q = \tau\mu q_i\), which is \(\tau\mu\) per tonne of plant \(i\)’s output. (iii) Firm \(f\)’s own bill is \(\tau\bar e\,Q_{EU,f}\) with \(Q_{EU,f} = \mu_f q_f\), so \(\partial(\tau\bar e\,Q_{EU,f})/\partial e_f = \tau\mu_f q_f \cdot q_f/Q\), which is \(\tau\mu_f\sigma_f\) per tonne of firm \(f\)’s output with \(\sigma_f = q_f/Q\). (iv) If the value charged is fixed for a period, the bill does not depend on any \(e_i\) within it.

Proposition 4. (i) \(\sum_i q_i t(e_i - \bar e) = t(\sum_i q_i e_i - \bar e\sum_i q_i) = 0\) with \(\bar e = \sum_i q_i e_i/\sum_i q_i\). (ii) A plant with \(e_i > \bar e\) pays \(t(e_i - \bar e)\) per tonne of output; a plant with \(e_i \le \bar e\) receives a rebate, which under netting of below-baseline emissions leaves a recognized price paid of zero (the reduction cannot be negative). (iii) The scrap-route plant has \(e_S < \bar e\), so its recognized deduction is zero and its EU bill is \(\tau e_S\); a BF-BOF tonne’s bill is \(\tau e_B - t(e_B - \bar e)\), which with \(t = \tau\) is \(\tau\bar e\), so routing saves \(\tau(\bar e - e_S)\). (iv) A tax at rate \(t\) is paid in full, \(t e_i\) per tonne of output, and induces \(e_i = e_{0i} - t/k_i\), the same intensity as a feebate at \(t\) (Stretton 2026e, Prop. 2).

Proposition 5. (i) \(\bar e_{c,s}\), \(p_{c,s}\) and \(t^{\mathrm{sig}}_{c,s}\) are sector aggregates. (ii) For \(\rho t \le \tau\), \(D(t) = c_0 + t^2/2k + (\tau - \rho t)(e_0 - t/k)\), so \(D'(t) = [(1+2\rho)t - \tau]/k - \rho e_0\) and \(D''(t) = (1+2\rho)/k > 0\). The stationary point is \(t = (\tau + \rho k e_0)/(1 + 2\rho)\). At \(\rho = 0\) it is \(\tau\). At \(\rho = 1\) it is \((\tau + k e_0)/3\), which exceeds \(\tau\) by \((k e_0 - 2\tau)/3 \ge 0\) when \(k e_0 \ge 2\tau\); then \(D\) is decreasing on \([0, \tau]\), and for \(t > \tau\) the liability is zero and \(D = c_0 + t^2/2k\) is increasing, so the minimum is at \(t = \tau\). \(D_{\rho=0}(\tau) - D_{\rho=1}(\tau) = \tau(e_0 - \tau/k)\). For \(0 < \rho < 1\) the minimizer is \(\min\{(\tau + \rho k e_0)/(1 + 2\rho), \tau/\rho\}\), which is at least \(\tau\) when \(k e_0 \ge 2\tau\). (iii) Per unit of output the country’s net cost is \(N(t) = t^2/2k + \mu(\tau - \rho t)(e_0 - t/k)\); \(N'(t) = t/k - \mu[\rho e_0 + \tau/k - 2\rho t/k] = 0\) gives equation 3, \(N''(t) = (1 + 2\rho\mu)/k > 0\), and \(\partial t^*/\partial\rho = \mu(k e_0 - 2\mu\tau)/(1 + 2\rho\mu)^2\). (iv) At \(\rho = 0\) the CBAM saving from \(t = \tau\) is \(\mu\tau\cdot\tau/k\) against a resource cost \(\tau^2/2k\), so the net gain is \((\tau^2/k)(\mu - 1/2)\). At \(\rho = 1\) the saving is the whole liability \(\mu\tau e_0\), so the net gain \(\mu\tau e_0 - \tau^2/2k\) is positive if and only if \(\mu > \tau/(2k e_0)\). The implied price per tonne abated of the relief is \(\mu\rho t\bar e/(t/k) = \mu\rho k\bar e\).

Proposition 6. The bill on a tonne from unit \(i\) is \(\tau[\lambda e_i + (1-\lambda)\bar e_{c,s}]\), so \(\partial(\cdot)/\partial e_i = \lambda\tau\) (ignoring unit \(i\)’s own small weight in \(\bar e_{c,s}\)), and the difference between supplying from \(B\) and from \(S\) is \(\lambda\tau(e_B - e_S)\).

All results were checked symbolically (2.Source/check_propositions.py).

Appendix C: Legal texts and status

The list comes from the EU Publications Office, from which the main texts were read on 31 October 2026, and from the Commission’s Have Your Say portal (initiative 14830), queried the same day.

Provisions quoted in the paper. Regulation 2023/956, Article 3(29): definition of carbon price; Article 30: reports on “international trade, including resource shuffling”; Annex II: direct emissions only for iron and steel and aluminum. Article 9(1)–(5) as replaced by Regulation 2025/2083: deduction for carbon price effectively paid, available where actual emissions are declared; netting of “any rebate or other form of compensation”; yearly default carbon prices “only where a carbon price was set by the rules applicable in the third country and a yearly default carbon price can be determined, including on a conservative basis”; the Commission “may” determine default carbon prices from 2027 “for third countries where carbon pricing rules are in place” and publish the methodology; implementing acts on conversion, evidence and examples of compensation. Regulation 2025/2083, recital 20 (annual average price “including on a conservative basis”) and recital 35 (ten-highest-intensity rule); Annex IV, point 4.1 (default values at country averages plus a mark-up set under Article 7(7)) and point 7 (region-specific adaptations). Directive 2023/959: CBAM factor 97.5 percent in 2026, 95 in 2027, 90 in 2028, 77.5 in 2029, 51.5 in 2030, 39 in 2031, 26.5 in 2032, 14 in 2033, none from 2034. Draft implementing regulation: recital 8 (binding mechanisms imposing obligations on all operators), Article 6 (conversion formulas), Article 8(1)(b)(ii) (below-baseline emissions as compensation), Article 8(2) (revenue-financed subsidies not netted under four conditions), and the 10 percent cap on Paris Agreement Article 6 credits.

Appendix D: Calibration data and code

Data. The default values are the Commission’s, as adopted under Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/2621 (European Commission 2025f); only the values in the Regulation are legally valid. For each of 119 countries and a residual “other countries” category, and for each CN code, the Regulation gives the direct, indirect and total default values, the values with the 2026, 2027 and 2028-onward mark-ups, and the production-route code that determines the CBAM benchmark. For steel and aluminum the indirect values are not applicable. The calibration uses direct values before mark-up for hot-rolled flat steel (CN 7208) and unwrought aluminum (CN 7601), extracted to ../1.1.OpenEconomyCarbonPricing/2.Source/CBAM-default-values-steel-aluminium-cement.csv and checked on 31 October 2026 against the Official Journal text for every country in Table 3 and Table 4. Every steel exporter in Table 3 carries route code (C), carbon steel by BF/BOF; unwrought aluminum carries (K), primary aluminum, or (L), secondary aluminum at 0.36 tCO₂/t, as the Regulation’s legend defines them. No World Bank internal data are used.

Stylized parameters. Certificate price €80/tCO₂. Full phase-in, with no free-allocation adjustment. Mark-up 30 percent. Scrap-EAF steel 0.4 tCO₂/t and BF-BOF steel 2.0 tCO₂/t in the worked example, against the IEA’s 0.3 and 2.2 (direct plus indirect) and 0.04 and 1.2 (direct) (International Energy Agency 2020). Secondary aluminum 0.36 tCO₂/t. Abatement cost \(c(e) = c_0 + \tfrac{k}{2}(e_0 - e)^2\) with \(k = 50/(0.3\,e_0)\), so that a rate of 50 cuts intensity by 30 percent and \(k e_0 = €166.7\)/tCO₂ for every exporter, as in paper 1.1 (Stretton 2026e). At €80 the induced intensity cut is 48 percent, so the condition \(k e_0 \ge 2\tau\) of Proposition 5(ii) holds.

Code. 2.Source/make_wp_figures.py reads the data, writes table_steel.csv and table_aluminium.csv (the source of Table 3 and Table 4) and draws Figure 1, Figure 2 and Figure 3. 2.Source/check_propositions.py checks Propositions 1–6 symbolically with SymPy and reproduces the numbers quoted from them: the €102 million saving in the worked example, the best-response rates of €8 and €21 at \(\mu = 0.1\), the 24 percent adoption threshold, and the €0.80 private incentive in the example of Proposition 3.
